purpose: Rifapentine is used to treat or prevent tuberculosis (TB), a serious infection that mainly affects the lungs. It is often used together with other antibiotics because TB requires combination treatment to work properly. It can also be used to prevent TB from becoming active in people who have been exposed to it.
how_it_works: Rifapentine works by blocking the TB bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive and multiply. Think of it like cutting off the bacteria's ability to copy its own instruction manual. Without that ability, the bacteria die off and the infection is controlled.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, loss of appetite, headache, and dizziness. You may also notice that your urine, sweat, saliva, or tears turn an orange-red color — this is harmless but can permanently stain contact lenses. Some people experience joint or muscle pain.
warnings: Rifapentine can cause serious liver problems, so tell your doctor right away if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain. It can interact with many medications, including birth control pills, making them less effective — use a backup method of contraception. Do not take it if you are pregnant without talking to your doctor, as it may harm the baby. Never stop taking this medication without talking to your doctor first, as stopping early can allow the bacteria to become resistant.
typical_dosing: The dose and schedule depend on whether you are treating active TB or preventing it. For prevention, a common regimen is once a week for 12 weeks, taken with another antibiotic called isoniazid. For active TB, it is usually taken twice a week during the intensive phase of treatment, then once a week. Always take it with food to help reduce stomach upset and improve how well your body absorbs it. Your doctor will give you a specific schedule — it is very important to follow it exactly.
